2017 began with my best friend's mother dying. She was like a second mother to me, helped raise me, influence who I became as a man, etc. It was quite difficult. In turn, helping my best friend clean out her house and find closure was super tough. He's still struggling...

As soon as I got back from my leave of absence to help him, I received the worst employment performance review I had ever got at a job. The company I was at kept going through strategy changes and it was impacting leadership, workflow, communication, etc.

I was given 60 days to straighten up or I would've been terminated. So crazy, given that I was working 70 hour work weeks, not sleeping, and barely spending any social time with friends or my wife. My job became my life and it was sorta destroying it.

A respite came in April when our whole department was suddenly laid off. (Thanks, Sinclair Broadcasting!) And I was suddenly in a position where I could take a break, recalibrate, and figure out exactly what the hell I was doing with my life.

It didn't really dawn on me how negatively affected I was by this employment situation until I was no longer attached to the company. I had lost weight, lost sleep, and lost a belief in my artistic capabilities. Basically, I began feeling like I couldn't write anymore.
But here we are, last few weeks of the year, and I've realized getting laid off was the best thing that happened to me in 2017.

It opened up doors to be able to contribute to a handful of outlets I'd never pictured myself writing for. I paid up my SAG dues and got a new manager. I've gotten paid more for articles than I ever thought I could. Most importantly, I found free time again.
In the next few days, I'll be disappearing from social media as I take a holiday sabbatical (and go to Mexico and eat all the tacos) so Happy Holidays and stuff, dear Twitter friends.

My grandfather was killed three years before I was born. A palm tree fell on his car as he was driving my grandmother to her surprise birthday party. It instantly killed him, put her in the hospital for six months. It was 1973.

Three years later, after my mother met a strapping young man in her apartment complex, she gave birth to me. The man in question (who ended up being a buddy to the Hell's Angels, a high school dropout, ex-convict, and brief 70s porn star) was my father.

My mom never went to therapy after her dad was killed. My grandmother didn't either. Instead, they lived in constant conflict w each other. The shock caused my mother to never visit my grandma in the hospital after the accident.

In turn, my grandmother held that over her head until the day she died. I grew up in that. Being taught that my dad was a piece of utter trash (it's a lesson that was continually taught to me throughout my life until he died) and being held down under this invisible fear.
As I grew into my teen years, this separation anxiety shifted to anger and then resentment towards my mother. I stopped telling her I loved her to make it easier to handle all of this.
I went from her to a girl I met at a club and she in turn dated like 7 other guys and a few girls behind-my-back only to have a miscarriage and claimed it was mine (it wasn't.)
My most recent ex, before I met my wife, I dated for 7 years and after that discovered that I was actually the guy she was cheating on her ACTUAL boyfriend with.

I didn't. Not until that last girl and that's when I figured that maybe, just maybe, it wasn't their fault. That I was to blame as well. So I went to a therapist and had a huge breakthrough during my time in therapy.
At this point, it was 6 years since she lost her husband and almost died. I remember being in the living room, the shag carpet, the odd yellow color of the kitchen walls.
But also, that's the moment that sparked my ongoing battle with separation anxiety. The death of my grandfather, who I never knew, directly affected me in this way.

I can list other ways it has, as well. But it's this factor right here that shaped the man I had become and led me down the various dysfunctional paths I've gone down. It's guided chaotic thoughts, mismanagement of money, horrible relationships, and huge bouts of self-doubt.
